title: Context, Languages and the Ancient Near East
bigQuestion: What changes when a reader tries to hear the Bible the way its first audience heard it?

story.title: The Plow That Opened a Library
story.kicker: In 1928 a farmer in northern Syria struck a stone, and a lost city began to speak again.
paragraphs: In the spring of 1928 a farmer was plowing a field near the Mediterranean coast of northern Syria, close to a bay called Minet el-Beida. His plow struck something hard. When he dug around it, he found a large stone slab. Under the slab was a stone-built tomb, very old, with pottery still inside. Local officials reported the find, and word reached archaeologists working for France, which governed Syria at the time.

The next year a French team led by Claude Schaeffer began digging at a mound nearby called Ras Shamra. Within weeks they found clay tablets covered in wedge-shaped marks. Some were written in the Akkadian script scholars already knew. Others used a script no one had seen before. It had only about thirty signs, which meant it was probably an alphabet.

Scholars worked on the new script quickly. By 1930 and 1931 several of them had deciphered it. The language was close to Hebrew and was named Ugaritic, after the city: the mound was ancient Ugarit, a trading port destroyed around 1185 BCE. Its scribes had written letters, business records, and long poems about gods.

Those poems named a high god called El, who sat at the head of an assembly of gods. They named El's sons, and a storm god named Baal who rode the clouds. Readers of the Hebrew Bible noticed at once that some of these words and pictures also appear in the Psalms. The Bible now had neighbors that could be read in their own words.

Decades later, Michael Heiser, a scholar of the Hebrew Bible and its related languages, made texts like these a central tool of his method. He argued that the Bible makes the most sense when read beside the world its first hearers lived in. This chapter looks at that method, its main tools, and the cautions that come with it.
story.think: Why might a poem from a neighboring city help, or mislead, someone trying to understand a psalm?

lessons.title: The Ancient Context First
lessons.mainIdea: Heiser's method was to read each biblical text in its ancient setting before asking what later traditions or modern readers made of it.
reading: Open to Psalm 82. The first verse pictures God standing in a gathering and judging among beings the psalm calls gods. Many modern readers find the verse puzzling. It does not fit what they expect a psalm to say. Heiser said that this puzzle was exactly where careful reading should begin. He urged readers not to smooth the verse over, but to ask what it would have meant to an Israelite who heard it sung.

Heiser called this reading in *context*. By context he meant the world of the writer and first audience: their language, their neighbors, their ideas about the heavens, and the other texts they knew. In The Unseen Realm (2015) he argued that many readers bring a filter to the Bible without noticing it. Some filters come from later church tradition. Others come from modern assumptions, such as the idea that ancient people must have thought about the world the way people do today.

Heiser did not say tradition is worthless. He said tradition should be tested against the text rather than read into it. This order of questions sits at the center of his method. First, what did the words mean in their own time? Only then, how have Jewish and Christian readers explained them since? Other scholars share this starting point. Most modern historical study of the Bible begins with the ancient setting.

Readers differ on how far to take this. Many Christians and Jews treat their long traditions of interpretation as trusted guides, not filters. They see the creeds, the rabbis or the church fathers as the community's best reading of the text. Heiser's approach is one voice in that conversation. It is the subject of this course, but it is not the only way people read.

words.d: the setting of a text: its language, time, place, culture and first audience
an explanation of what a text means
the teachings and readings a community passes down over generations

Asking who first heard a psalm sung

lessons.title: The Naked Bible Idea
lessons.mainIdea: Heiser used the name Naked Bible for his aim of reading Scripture stripped of later filters, and he named his long-running podcast after it.
reading: From 2014 to 2023 Heiser hosted the Naked Bible Podcast. Episodes often worked slowly through one book of the Bible, sometimes a few verses at a time. The name described his goal. He wanted to read the Bible stripped of the layers readers had wrapped around it, so that its own words and its own ancient world could be seen clearly.

Take Job 1:6. It tells of a day when the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD, and the satan came among them. Many readers picture the devil at a church meeting. Heiser asked readers to set that picture aside for a moment. In the Hebrew text, he pointed out, the word satan has the definite article, the satan, so it reads like a title meaning the adversary or accuser. The scene looks like a royal court, with members reporting to their king.

The phrase sons of God in Job is an example of what Heiser meant by letting the text speak. In Job 38:7 the sons of God shout for joy when the earth is founded, before humans exist. So, Heiser argued, in Job the phrase must name heavenly beings. Seeing this, he said, helps a reader notice the same phrase elsewhere, including Genesis 6:2.

A fair reader will notice a limit to the Naked Bible idea. No one reads with no filters at all. Every reader brings a language, a translation and questions. Heiser's critics and friends alike have said so. The idea is best taken as a direction to work in, checking one's own assumptions, rather than a claim that any reader can reach a perfectly bare text.

words.d: a Hebrew phrase (bene elohim) that in Job names heavenly beings in God's court
a Hebrew word meaning adversary or accuser; in Job 1 it appears with 'the', like a title
something a reader takes for granted without checking

look.title: Two Pictures of One Scene
look.text: Picture A: a modern reader imagines Job 1:6 as the devil sneaking into a church service. Picture B: a reader of ancient court scenes imagines a king on a throne, with officials arriving to give reports, and one of them, called the adversary, raising a charge.
look.prompt: Which details in Job 1:6 support Picture B? What does a reader bring to the text to get Picture A?

check.q: What did the name Naked Bible describe?
choices: A plan to read the Bible without any translation
A goal of reading the text stripped of later filters
A new version of the Bible Heiser translated
A rule that only experts may read the Bible

check.q: Why did Heiser argue the sons of God in Job are heavenly beings?
choices: Because 1 Enoch says so in chapter 1
Because Job 38:7 has them shouting for joy when the earth was founded, before humans
Because the Ugaritic tablets name Job

lessons.title: Languages as Tools
lessons.mainIdea: Heiser was trained in Hebrew and related ancient languages, and he used them to notice words that translations can hide.
reading: Heiser earned his PhD in Hebrew Bible and Semitic Studies at the University of Wisconsin–Madison in 2004. Semitic languages are a family that includes Hebrew, Aramaic, Akkadian, Ugaritic and Arabic. Knowing several of them lets a scholar compare how a word is used across neighboring peoples. His dissertation studied the divine council in Jewish writings from the Second Temple period, roughly 500 BCE to 70 CE.

Here is one reason languages matter. Psalm 29:1 in the King James Version begins, Give unto the LORD, O ye mighty. The Hebrew behind O ye mighty is bene elim, which can be read as sons of gods or heavenly beings. Some modern translations render it heavenly beings or divine beings. The English word mighty is not wrong, but it hides a connection that a Hebrew reader would hear at once.

A *translation* always involves choices. Translators must decide whether to keep a strange phrase or make it smoother. Heiser often told listeners to check more than one English translation. He also encouraged them to use reference tools that show the Hebrew or Greek word behind the English. Much of his career was spent at Logos, a company that makes Bible study software, working on such tools.

Languages do not settle every question. Two experts can read the same Hebrew word and disagree. What language study does is show the range of what a word could mean. It also shows which meanings are likely in a given setting. Heiser's arguments often begin there, and so do his critics' replies.

words.d: a family of related languages including Hebrew, Aramaic, Akkadian, Ugaritic and Arabic
a text carried from one language into another, which always involves choices
a Hebrew phrase in Psalm 29:1 that can mean sons of gods or heavenly beings
the era of the rebuilt temple in Jerusalem, about 500 BCE to 70 CE

look.title: One Verse, Two Renderings
look.text: King James Version (1611), Psalm 29:1: Give unto the LORD, O ye mighty, give unto the LORD glory and strength. Several modern translations, described in our own words: they address the call to heavenly beings or divine beings, following the Hebrew bene elim.
look.prompt: How might a reader's picture of this psalm change depending on which rendering they read?

check.q: Which language is NOT part of the Semitic family?
check.why: Greek is an Indo-European language. Hebrew, Aramaic, Akkadian and Ugaritic are Semitic.

check.q: What Hebrew phrase lies behind the King James words O ye mighty in Psalm 29:1?
check.why: The Hebrew is bene elim, which can mean sons of gods or heavenly beings.

check.q: What did Heiser's dissertation (2004) study?
choices: The history of the King James Version
The divine council in Second Temple Jewish writings
check.why: His University of Wisconsin–Madison dissertation studied the divine council in late canonical and non-canonical Second Temple Jewish literature.

lessons.title: A City Found by a Plow
lessons.mainIdea: Ugarit, a port city in Syria destroyed around 1185 BCE, left clay tablets in a Hebrew-like language that scholars use to understand the Bible's world.
reading: Ugarit stood on the coast of what is now northern Syria, near the modern city of Latakia. It was a busy trading port during the Late Bronze Age. Ships and caravans linked it to Egypt, Cyprus, the Hittites and Mesopotamia. Around 1185 BCE the city was destroyed and never rebuilt. Its ruins became the mound called *Ras Shamra*.

Excavations that began in 1929 uncovered palaces, temples and houses full of tablets. Scribes had written in several languages. The most important new one was *Ugaritic*, written in a wedge-shaped alphabet of about thirty letters pressed into clay. Most of the tablets date from roughly 1400 to 1185 BCE. That makes them centuries older than most scholars' dates for the written books of the Hebrew Bible.

Ugaritic is a close relative of Hebrew. Many words are nearly the same, and poems in both languages use similar patterns, such as saying one thing twice in slightly different words. Because of this, the tablets became a major tool for Hebrew Bible scholars. They help explain rare Hebrew words and poetic habits.

Ugarit was not Israel, and its people were not Israelites. Scholars use it as a window onto the wider Canaanite world that Israel's writers knew and often argued against. Heiser used it that way too. He said the tablets show the religious vocabulary of the region, which helps a reader notice when a biblical writer uses that vocabulary on purpose.

words.d: the modern Arabic name of the mound in Syria that holds the ruins of Ugarit
the language of Ugarit, close to Hebrew, written in a cuneiform alphabet of about thirty letters
writing made of wedge-shaped marks pressed into wet clay
a period in the ancient Near East, roughly 1550 to 1200 BCE

lessons.title: El and His Council
lessons.mainIdea: Ugaritic poems picture the high god El leading an assembly of gods called his sons, a picture Heiser compared to the Bible's divine council.
reading: In the Ugaritic poems, *El* is the aged, wise king of the gods. He is called father and creator, and he lives at a distant mountain where the gods come to meet him. The gods around him form an assembly. The tablets use phrases that mean the assembly of the gods and the assembly of the sons of El. Scholars call this kind of gathering a *divine council*.

One poem refers to the seventy sons of Athirat, El's wife. Heiser, like several scholars before him, noticed the number. Genesis 10 lists the nations after the flood, and Jewish tradition counts them as seventy. Deuteronomy 32:8, in its oldest known Hebrew copy, says God divided the nations according to the number of the sons of God. Heiser argued that a reader in Israel's world would hear these ideas together.

Heiser did not say that Israel borrowed its beliefs from Ugarit. He argued that the Bible's writers shared a vocabulary with their neighbors, like a family of languages sharing words. Then, he said, they used it to make their own claims. In the Hebrew Bible, the council belongs to Israel's God, and its members are his creations.

Other scholars read the parallels differently. Mark S. Smith, for example, has argued that Israel's early religion grew out of this Canaanite setting, and that El and Yahweh were once thought of as separate gods before being joined. Chapter 30 looks at that debate. For now, the point is shared ground: most scholars agree the council idea appears in both Ugarit and the Bible.

words.d: the high god and king of the gods in the Ugaritic texts; also a Hebrew word for God or a god
the assembly of heavenly beings gathered around a chief god, found in Ugaritic texts and, many scholars argue, in the Bible
El's wife in the Ugaritic texts, related to the name Asherah in the Bible

look.title: Seventy, Three Times
look.text: Ugarit: a poem mentions the seventy sons of Athirat. Genesis 10: Jewish tradition counts seventy nations in the list. Deuteronomy 32:8, oldest Hebrew copy: the nations are divided by the number of the sons of God.
look.prompt: Does a shared number prove a connection? What else would you want to know before deciding?

check.q: In the Ugaritic texts, who leads the assembly of the gods?
check.why: El is the aged king of the gods, and the assembly gathers around him.

check.q: What did Heiser argue about Israel and Ugarit's vocabulary?
choices: The two had no words in common
Israel's writers shared the vocabulary and used it to make their own claims
Ugarit borrowed from the book of Deuteronomy
check.why: Heiser described a shared vocabulary put to Israel's own use, not simple borrowing.

check.q: How does Mark S. Smith's reading differ from Heiser's?
choices: Smith says the council appears only in the New Testament
Smith argues Israel's religion grew from its Canaanite setting and that El and Yahweh were once separate
Smith agrees with Heiser on every point
check.why: Smith has argued for a development from Canaanite religion, including an early distinction between El and Yahweh.

lessons.title: Psalm 82 Beside Ugarit
lessons.mainIdea: Heiser read Psalm 82 as Israel's God judging the members of his council, while other readers take the gods there to be human judges or Israel at Sinai.
reading: Psalm 82:1 in Hebrew says God stands in the adat el, which can be translated the council of El or the divine council. The phrase closely matches Ugaritic phrases for the assembly of the gods. The psalm goes on to accuse the gods of judging unjustly and failing the weak and the orphan. Then God pronounces a sentence: though they are gods and sons of the Most High, they will die like humans.

Heiser argued that the gods in Psalm 82 are real members of a heavenly council. In his reading, God had placed them over the nations, and they ruled badly. This, he said, ties Psalm 82 to Deuteronomy 32:8. He made this one of the anchor texts of The Unseen Realm (2015). He pointed out that the setting is a council like the one known from Ugarit, and that the sentence to die like humans makes the most sense if they are not human.

Other readings have a long history. Some Jewish and Christian interpreters read the gods as human judges, since judges act in God's name. When Jesus quotes Psalm 82:6 in John 10:34, some readers take him to mean human leaders. An old rabbinic reading applies the psalm to Israel at Mount Sinai. Many modern scholars, including some who disagree with Heiser elsewhere, share his view that the psalm describes divine beings.

Setting Psalm 82 beside Ugarit does not decide the question alone. It shows that the phrase council of El had a known meaning in the region. Readers still must weigh the rest of the psalm, John 10, and how their own tradition has read it. A parallel opens the question; it does not close it.

words.d: a Hebrew phrase in Psalm 82:1 meaning the council or congregation of El (God)
a title for God (Hebrew Elyon) used in Psalm 82:6 and Deuteronomy 32:8
a passage an interpreter treats as a key to reading other passages

look.title: The Sentence in Psalm 82
look.text: I have said, Ye are gods; and all of you are children of the most High. But ye shall die like men, and fall like one of the princes.
look.prompt: How does the phrase die like men support Heiser's reading? How might a reader who sees human judges here explain it?

check.q: Which Ugaritic idea does the phrase adat el in Psalm 82:1 resemble?
check.why: Adat el closely matches Ugaritic phrases for the assembly or council of the gods.

check.q: According to Heiser, who are the gods in Psalm 82?
choices: Members of a heavenly council placed over the nations
check.why: Heiser read them as divine beings who ruled the nations badly and are sentenced to die like humans.

check.q: Which New Testament passage quotes Psalm 82:6?
check.why: In John 10:34 Jesus quotes Psalm 82:6. Readers differ on what he meant by it.

lessons.title: Psalm 29 and the Storm
lessons.mainIdea: Many scholars think Psalm 29 uses the language of Canaanite storm poems, and Heiser saw such borrowings as claims that Israel's God held the titles given to Baal.
reading: Psalm 29 describes a great storm. The voice of the LORD is over the waters. It thunders, breaks the cedars of Lebanon, and shakes the wilderness. The psalm begins by calling on the bene elim, the heavenly beings, to give glory to the LORD. It ends with the LORD enthroned over the flood as king.

Since the discovery of Ugarit, many scholars have noticed how much Psalm 29 sounds like poems about *Baal*, the Canaanite storm god. At Ugarit, Baal thunders, rules from his mountain, defeats the Sea, and is proclaimed king. Some scholars think Psalm 29 was adapted from an older Canaanite hymn. Others think it was written in Israel using the region's familiar storm language.

Heiser read passages like this as polemic. A *polemic* is writing that argues against a rival view. In his books he pointed to Baal's title rider of the clouds in the Ugaritic poems. Then he noted that the Hebrew Bible gives Israel's God similar imagery, as in Psalm 68:4 and Psalm 104:3. The message, he argued, was that the LORD, not Baal, is the true ruler of the storm and the sea.

Readers who do not accept every part of Heiser's work often agree on this point. The idea that biblical writers answered Canaanite religion with its own imagery is common in scholarship. Where people differ is how much the imagery was borrowed, adapted or simply shared, and what that says about Israel's early beliefs.

words.d: the Canaanite storm god in the Ugaritic poems, called king and rider of the clouds
writing that argues against a rival idea or belief
a title of Baal at Ugarit; the Hebrew Bible uses similar imagery for Israel's God

look.title: Same Storm, Different King
look.text: Ugaritic poems: Baal's voice thunders, he rides the clouds, defeats the Sea and is named king. Psalm 29: the LORD's voice thunders over the waters, breaks the cedars, and the LORD sits enthroned over the flood as king forever.
look.prompt: If you were an Israelite who knew the Baal poems, what claim would Psalm 29 seem to be making?

check.q: What is a polemic?
choices: Writing that argues against a rival view
check.why: A polemic argues against a rival idea. Heiser read storm imagery in the Psalms this way.

check.q: Which Canaanite god is called rider of the clouds at Ugarit?
check.why: Baal, the storm god, carries this title in the Ugaritic poems.

check.q: On what point do many scholars who differ from Heiser still agree with him?
choices: That Psalm 29 was written at Ugarit
That biblical writers answered Canaanite religion using its own imagery
That 1 Enoch is part of every Bible
That Baal and El are the same god
check.why: The idea that Israel's writers used and redirected Canaanite imagery is common in scholarship.

sections.title: Sages, Watchers and a Hebrew Word

lessons.title: The Apkallu of Mesopotamia
lessons.mainIdea: Heiser, building on Amar Annus, argued that Genesis 6 and 1 Enoch turn Mesopotamia's honored sages, the apkallu, into rebels who spread harmful knowledge.
reading: In Mesopotamian tradition the *apkallu* were seven wise beings who lived before the great flood. They were said to have brought people the arts of civilization, such as writing, building and crafts. Assyrian palace carvings from the 800s BCE show figures often identified as apkallu, some dressed in a fish-shaped cloak and some with a bird's head. A Babylonian priest named Berossus, writing in Greek around 290 BCE, told of a sage called Oannes who came from the sea to teach humans.

In Mesopotamia these sages were heroes. Kings liked to link their wisdom to them. Some texts describe later sages, after the flood, as only partly apkallu, mixed with human descent. In 2010 the scholar Amar Annus published an article comparing these traditions with the *Watchers* of 1 Enoch.

Heiser drew on Annus's work in Reversing Hermon (2017). He argued that Genesis 6:1–4 and 1 Enoch retell the Mesopotamian story in reverse. In 1 Enoch 6–8, heavenly Watchers come down, have children with human women, and teach forbidden knowledge such as weapon-making. The sages Mesopotamia honored become, in the Jewish telling, the source of trouble. Heiser saw this as polemic against Babylon's pride.

Not every scholar agrees on the details. Some think the links are clear; others think the traditions grew separately from a shared stock of flood-era stories. Checking the argument means reading the actual texts on both sides, in good translations, not only summaries of them.

words.d: in Mesopotamian tradition, seven wise beings before the flood who taught people the arts of civilization
in 1 Enoch, heavenly beings who came down to earth and did wrong; the word comes from Daniel 4 and 1 Enoch
a Babylonian priest who wrote a history in Greek around 290 BCE
an ancient Jewish book whose oldest parts date to about 300–200 BCE; canonical in the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox churches

look.title: What the Watchers Taught
look.text: The Watcher Azazel taught people to make swords, knives, shields and armor. He showed them metals and how to work them, and taught them to make bracelets, ornaments and eye makeup, and how to use precious stones and dyes.

look.prompt: In Mesopotamia, bringing crafts to people made the sages heroes. How does 1 Enoch 8 treat the same kind of teaching?

choices: Seven wise beings before the flood who taught the arts of civilization
The sons of Athirat at Ugarit
check.why: The apkallu were honored pre-flood sages. The pyramids claim is not in the texts.

check.q: Whose 2010 article did Heiser build on when comparing the apkallu and the Watchers?
check.why: Amar Annus published the comparison of the apkallu and the Watchers in 2010.

check.q: According to Heiser, how does the Jewish telling treat what Mesopotamia honored?
choices: It turns them into the source of trouble

check.why: Heiser argued Genesis 6 and 1 Enoch reverse the story, so the knowledge-bringers become rebels.

lessons.title: Elohim: A Word About Where
lessons.mainIdea: Heiser argued that the Hebrew word elohim names beings whose home is the spirit world, not a list of qualities that only the God of Israel has.
reading: The Hebrew word *elohim* is usually translated God when it refers to the God of Israel. But the Hebrew Bible uses the same word for other beings too. Psalm 82 uses it for the members of the council. Deuteronomy 32:17 uses it for the shedim, spirit beings to whom Israel wrongly sacrificed. In 1 Samuel 28:13, a woman at Endor uses the word for the spirit of the dead prophet Samuel.

If elohim meant all-powerful, eternal creator, these uses would make little sense. Heiser concluded that the word says where a being belongs, not what it is like. He called it a word about place of residence. An elohim, in his reading, is a being whose proper home is the unseen world. The God of Israel, the council, lesser spirits and the dead could all be described with the word in that sense.

This idea shaped much of his work. It lets a reader take the plural uses of elohim seriously without concluding that the Bible teaches many equal gods. The word marks a realm, and inside that realm there are very different kinds of beings, from the God of Israel to the spirits of the dead.

Some scholars welcome this as a helpful description of how the word is used. Others think it is too neat, and that elohim also carried ideas of power and rank, not only place. Many traditional readers explain the plural uses differently, as the word applied loosely to judges, idols or false gods. Knowing these options lets a student test each against the passages.

words.d: a Hebrew word used for the God of Israel and also for other beings of the unseen world
a Hebrew word in Deuteronomy 32:17 for spirit beings Israel wrongly sacrificed to
Heiser's description of elohim as a word that tells where a being belongs

look.title: One Word, Many Beings
look.text: And the king said unto her, Be not afraid: for what sawest thou? And the woman said unto Saul, I saw gods ascending out of the earth.
look.prompt: The word translated gods here is elohim, and it refers to Samuel's spirit. How does this verse support Heiser's idea of a place word?

check.q: In Heiser's view, what does the word elohim tell about a being?
choices: That its proper home is the unseen world
check.why: Heiser described elohim as a place-of-residence word: it tells where a being belongs.

check.q: In which passage is elohim used for the spirit of the prophet Samuel?
check.why: In 1 Samuel 28:13 the woman at Endor calls Samuel's spirit elohim.

check.q: What is one criticism of Heiser's place-of-residence idea?
choices: It is found only in Greek
It may be too neat, since elohim also carried ideas of power and rank
check.why: Some scholars think the word also carried ideas of power and rank, not place alone.

lessons.title: Unique Among the Elohim
lessons.mainIdea: Heiser said the God of Israel is an elohim, but no other elohim is the God of Israel, because only he is uncreated and the creator of the rest.
reading: If many beings can be called elohim, what makes the God of Israel different? Heiser answered with a phrase he used in The Unseen Realm (2015). He called Israel's God *species-unique*. Every member of the council is an elohim, but only one elohim is Yahweh. In Heiser's reading, Yahweh stands alone because he is uncreated, all-powerful and the maker of every other being.

Heiser pointed to verses that compare the LORD to other heavenly beings. Psalm 89:6–7 asks who in the skies can be compared with the LORD, and who among the heavenly beings is like him. Nehemiah 9:6 says the host of heaven worships him. Exodus 15:11 asks who is like the LORD among the gods. To Heiser, these verses only make sense if the other beings exist. Yet in each one the LORD has no equal.

This is why Heiser was uneasy with the word *monotheism* as it is often used today. He argued that if monotheism means only that no other spiritual beings exist, the Hebrew Bible does not fit it. If it means that only one being is God in the full sense, then he believed the Hebrew Bible fits it well.

Other scholars use other labels. Some say henotheism, the worship of one god without denying others. Some say monolatry, the worship of one god alone. Many Jewish and Christian readers simply say monotheism, meaning one God and created angels. Heiser's point was about describing the texts carefully, whatever label is used.

words.d: Heiser's term for the God of Israel as an elohim unlike all others: uncreated and creator of the rest
the personal name of the God of Israel in the Hebrew Bible, shown as the LORD in many English Bibles
belief in one God; scholars define it in different ways
worship of one god without denying that other gods exist

look.title: Who Is Like Him?
look.text: For who in the heaven can be compared unto the LORD? who among the sons of the mighty can be likened unto the LORD?
look.prompt: What does this question assume about the heavens? How does it support the idea of a species-unique God?

check.q: What did Heiser mean by calling Israel's God species-unique?
choices: That he is one of many equal gods
That he is a human king
That he is an elohim, but uncreated and creator of all others
That he is the same as Baal
check.why: Heiser said Yahweh is an elohim, but no other elohim is Yahweh, because only he is uncreated.

check.q: Which verse asks who among the sons of the mighty can be likened to the LORD?
check.why: Psalm 89:6 compares the LORD to heavenly beings and finds none like him.

check.q: What is henotheism?
choices: Worship of one god without denying that other gods exist
Belief that no spiritual beings exist
check.why: Henotheism means worshiping one god while not denying others exist.

lessons.title: What Comparison Can Show
lessons.mainIdea: Comparing the Bible with neighboring texts can show shared words and pictures, and it can also show where the Bible says something different.
reading: Comparison works like holding two maps side by side. When scholars set Psalm 82 beside Ugaritic council scenes, they learn that council of El was a known phrase. When they set Genesis 6 beside the apkallu, they notice that similar ideas are valued very differently. Both kinds of results matter.

Heiser stressed the differences as much as the likenesses. At Ugarit, El is the old king and Baal is a younger god who fights to become king. In the Hebrew Bible, Heiser noted, both roles belong to one God. Israel's God is the ancient king of the council and also the one who rides the clouds and rules the sea. The same pictures are used, but the claim is new.

Comparison also helps with words. A rare Hebrew word may appear only once or twice in the Bible, which makes its meaning hard to pin down. If the same word appears many times in Ugaritic or Akkadian texts, the context there can suggest a meaning. Dictionaries of biblical Hebrew now use such evidence.

Comparison does not tell a reader whether a text is true. It tells how a text fits its world. That is why Heiser's method can be studied and discussed by readers of any faith or of none. Each reader can then decide what to make of the results, drawing on their own tradition or none.

words.d: studying a text by setting it beside related texts from the same region and time
a likeness between two texts, such as a shared phrase or image
the Semitic language of ancient Babylon and Assyria, written in cuneiform

look.title: Likeness and Difference
look.text: At Ugarit: El is the aged king of the council; Baal, a younger god, rides the clouds and battles the Sea. In the Hebrew Bible, as Heiser read it: one God is ancient king of the council (Daniel 7:9 pictures an Ancient of Days) and also rides the heavens (Psalm 68:4).
look.prompt: What is the same in the two columns? What is different, and why might the difference be the main point?

check.q: According to Heiser, how does the Hebrew Bible handle the roles of El and Baal?
choices: It never mentions clouds or councils
It keeps El and Baal as two equal gods
It gives both roles to Moses
It gives both roles to one God
check.why: Heiser noted that the Hebrew Bible places the old king's role and the cloud-rider's role in one God.

check.q: How can Ugaritic texts help with a rare Hebrew word?
choices: They prove the Bible is true
They were written by the same authors
Many uses of the same word there can suggest its meaning
check.why: A word used often in a related language can suggest what a rare Hebrew word meant.

check.q: What can comparison NOT tell a reader?
choices: Where two texts use the same image
How a text fits its ancient world
Whether a religious claim is true
check.why: Comparison shows how a text fits its world; it does not settle questions of faith.

lessons.title: Beware of Parallelomania
lessons.mainIdea: Samuel Sandmel coined parallelomania in 1961 for overdoing likenesses between texts and assuming one must have borrowed from the other.
reading: In December 1961 Samuel Sandmel, a Jewish scholar of the New Testament and early Judaism, gave the presidential address to the Society of Biblical Literature. It was published the next year. He gave it the title Parallelomania. He used the word to name a habit he saw in scholarship. Scholars would find a likeness between two texts, overstate it, and then claim one text copied from the other, as if the direction of borrowing were obvious.

Sandmel did not say comparison is useless. He said a likeness is only the start of the work. A shared phrase might come from a shared culture, from a common older source, or from chance. And a phrase can mean something different in each text. A careful reader studies each text in its own setting before deciding what a likeness means.

The same caution applies to claims about Heiser's subjects. Some popular books say Mesopotamian carvings of apkallu show ancient astronauts, or that giants built the pyramids. Heiser rejected such claims. He publicly challenged Zecharia Sitchin, whose books claimed Sumerian texts described visitors from another planet. Heiser argued that Sitchin's readings did not match the actual Sumerian and Akkadian words.

Readers can apply Sandmel's test to Heiser's own comparisons too. Is the likeness real in the original languages? Is the direction of influence shown, or only assumed? Asking these questions is not an attack on a scholar. It is how every serious argument in the field is checked.

words.d: Samuel Sandmel's 1961 word for overstating likenesses between texts and assuming one borrowed from the other
the effect one text or culture has on another; scholars must show it, not assume it
a large professional association of scholars who study the Bible, founded in 1880

look.title: Check the Claim
look.text: A website says: An Assyrian carving shows a figure with a fish-shaped cloak and a bucket. This proves visitors from space taught ancient people. A reader checks: the carvings are usually identified as apkallu, the wise sages of Mesopotamian tradition. The texts about the apkallu call them sages sent by the gods, and say nothing of other planets.
look.prompt: Using Sandmel's cautions, list two steps the reader took and one more step they could take.

check.q: What did Samuel Sandmel mean by parallelomania?

check.q: Whose claims about Sumerian texts did Heiser publicly challenge?
check.why: Heiser argued that Zecharia Sitchin's ancient-astronaut readings did not match the Sumerian and Akkadian texts.

check.q: Which question follows Sandmel's advice when checking a comparison?
choices: Is the direction of influence shown, or only assumed?
Does the comparison fit my beliefs?
check.why: Sandmel warned against assuming who borrowed from whom. Influence must be shown.

At Qumran by the Dead Sea

Read the Bible only through church creeds

review.q: The phrase adat el in Psalm 82:1 is closest in meaning to which phrase?

review.q: In the Ugaritic texts, who is the storm god that fights the Sea?

choices: It is a word about where a being belongs

choices: Some traditional Jewish and Christian interpreters
